cards.term: I see it a bit differently
cards.meaning: A gentle way of saying you disagree, by presenting your view as a different perspective.
cards.nuance: Calm and non-confrontational; it frames disagreement as viewpoint, not error. Follow it with your reasoning, or it can sound evasive.

uses.where: Design review · disagreeing with a lead
uses.sentence: I see it a bit differently — I think users will miss the search bar if we hide it.
uses.highlight: I see it a bit differently
uses.tip: Give your reason straight after the dash.

uses.sentence: I see it a bit differently, actually — I thought the ending was hopeful.
uses.highlight: I see it a bit differently
uses.tip: Adding “actually” keeps it light and conversational.

uses.where: Reply in a shared doc comment
uses.sentence: I see this a bit differently: the delay came from approvals, not engineering.
uses.highlight: I see this a bit differently
uses.tip: In writing, a colon and one clear reason works best.

origin.summary: No single origin story: it is plain English. It relies on “see” meaning “understand or judge”, a sense recorded since medieval English, plus the modern softener “a bit”.

timeline.text: “Sēon” means to see with the eyes.
“See” gains the sense “understand, perceive mentally”.
Hedges like “a bit” soften disagreement in polite speech.

cards.pitfall: If you never explain how you see it, people may assume you have no real objection.

cards.meaning: To argue against an idea, even one you may support, to test how strong it is.
cards.nuance: Signals that your objection is a thought experiment, not personal. Overused, it can look like a shield for opinions you actually hold.

uses.sentence: Let me play devil’s advocate — what happens if the competitor drops their price first?
uses.tip: Follow it with a genuine question, not a lecture.

uses.sentence: Just to play devil’s advocate, maybe the new neighbours didn’t know about the noise rules.
uses.tip: Useful for calming a pile-on by offering another side.

uses.sentence: To play devil’s advocate for a moment, the four-day week may not suit every industry.
uses.tip: “For a moment” signals you’ll return to your main argument.

origin.summary: From the Catholic Church’s advocatus diaboli, an official who argued against making someone a saint. The office was formalised in 1587 under Pope Sixtus V.

timeline.text: Sixtus V formalises the office of Promoter of the Faith, nicknamed “devil’s advocate”.
English writers use “devil’s advocate” for anyone arguing the opposing side.
John Paul II greatly reduces the office’s role in canonisation.

cards.pitfall: Playing devil’s advocate on sensitive personal topics can come across as insensitive.

cards.meaning: A polite opener before disagreeing with or criticising someone, especially someone senior.
cards.nuance: Literally respectful, but often heard as a warning that criticism is coming. Tone matters: said coldly, it can sound sarcastic or even rude.

uses.sentence: With all due respect, the survey only covered twenty customers, so I’d be careful drawing conclusions.
uses.tip: Keep the criticism factual so the respect feels real.

uses.sentence: With all due respect, Uncle Raj, the bank won’t lend us money because of a lucky number.
uses.tip: With family it can sound stiff — a smile helps.

uses.sentence: With all due respect, the policy you cite does not apply to orders placed before March.
uses.tip: In writing, follow it with evidence, not emotion.

origin.summary: Built from “due respect”, meaning the respect someone is owed. It became a set formula in legal and parliamentary speech, where speakers must disagree courteously; its edgy, ironic use is more modern.

timeline.text: “Due” (owed, proper) comes into English from Old French.
“With due respect” used as a courtesy in courts and parliaments.
Widely recognised as a signal that disagreement is coming.

cards.pitfall: Many listeners hear “with all due respect” as “I don’t respect this at all” — use it sparingly.

cards.meaning: I understand your point, but I still disagree or have a concern.
cards.nuance: Shows you’ve listened before pushing back. If the “but” comes too fast, it can sound like you didn’t really hear them at all.

uses.sentence: I hear you, but if we skip testing now we’ll spend twice as long fixing bugs later.
uses.tip: Briefly restate their point first to prove you heard it.

uses.where: Friend wants to quit their job
uses.sentence: I hear you, but maybe line up something new before you hand in your notice?
uses.tip: Ending with a question keeps it supportive.

uses.sentence: I hear you, but the client asked for this specifically, so I’d keep it in.
uses.tip: Fine in chat; in formal email, “I understand, however” fits better.

origin.summary: “I hear you” for “I understand you” is 20th-century American speech. It gained weight through counselling’s “active listening”, a term coined by Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957.

timeline.text: “I hear you” used in US speech to mean “I understand”.
Rogers and Farson describe “active listening”, encouraging people to reflect back what they hear.
“I hear you, but” is a common softener before disagreement.

cards.pitfall: Used every time, it becomes a verbal tic that signals you’re about to dismiss the other person.

cards.term: Let me push back on that
cards.meaning: I want to challenge or question what was just said.
cards.nuance: Direct but professional; it names the disagreement openly. In some cultures it can feel more confrontational than English speakers intend.

uses.sentence: Let me push back on that a little — adding three features now puts the launch at risk.
uses.tip: “A little” makes it sound collaborative rather than combative.

uses.sentence: I’m going to push back on that — a 5 a.m. flight is not a holiday.
uses.tip: With friends, a joke takes the edge off.

uses.sentence: I’d push back on the assumption that remote teams are less productive; our data suggests otherwise.
uses.tip: Point to evidence so it reads as reasoned, not stubborn.

origin.summary: From the physical image of pushing against a force. The figurative sense of resisting a plan or argument, and the noun “pushback”, spread in American English in the second half of the 20th century.

timeline.text: Literal “push back”: to shove something in the opposite direction.
Figurative “resist, object” sense appears in US politics and business.
Standard workplace vocabulary for respectful disagreement.

cards.pitfall: In British English, “push back” can also mean postpone (“push the meeting back”) — context matters.

cards.meaning: To accept that you hold different opinions and stop arguing about it.
cards.nuance: A graceful exit from a debate that’s going nowhere. Said abruptly, it can sound like “I’m done listening to you.”

uses.where: Long debate over a tool choice
uses.sentence: We clearly won’t settle this today, so let’s agree to disagree and let the pilot data decide.
uses.tip: Name a next step so the disagreement doesn’t just linger.

uses.sentence: You think Messi’s better, I think Ronaldo is — let’s agree to disagree and order food.
uses.tip: Perfect for friendly arguments with no right answer.

uses.sentence: I think we’ll have to agree to disagree on this point, but I appreciate you hearing me out.
uses.tip: Adding thanks keeps the relationship warm.

origin.summary: Recorded in the 1700s and associated with Methodist founder John Wesley, who used it about doctrinal differences with fellow preacher George Whitefield. The older “agree to differ” means the same.

timeline.text: “Agree to differ” used in English for accepting different views.
Wesley’s sermon on Whitefield’s death uses “agree to disagree” for minor doctrinal differences.
A standard, friendly way to end an argument.

cards.pitfall: Used to shut down a conversation the other person still cares about, it can feel dismissive.

cards.meaning: An idea or remark worth thinking about carefully.
cards.nuance: A soft way to raise a concern without demanding a decision. It can also be a polite way of saying “I’m not convinced yet.”

uses.sentence: I won’t block the plan, but here’s some food for thought: our biggest client hates long contracts.
uses.tip: Great for raising a risk without derailing the decision.

uses.sentence: That’s real food for thought — I hadn’t considered moving closer to work.
uses.tip: Shows appreciation even if you haven’t decided anything.

uses.sentence: As food for thought, try tracking how many meetings you could have replaced with an email.
uses.tip: Works as a gentle sign-off that invites reflection.

origin.summary: A metaphor of ideas as nourishment for the mind. The exact phrase is recorded in English by the early 19th century, building on older expressions like “food for the mind”.

timeline.text: Writers describe reading and ideas as “food for the mind”.
“Food for thought” appears in print in its modern sense.
A common, gentle way to flag an idea for reflection.

cards.pitfall: Saying “just some food for thought” after a strong criticism can sound passive-aggressive.

cards.meaning: I accept that part of your argument is reasonable, but I still have a different view.
cards.nuance: Gives genuine credit before disagreeing, which lowers defensiveness. Sincerity matters — if you don’t mean “fair”, people notice.

uses.sentence: That’s a fair point, however her portfolio shows she learns new tools quickly.
uses.tip: Name what’s fair about their point to make it sincere.

uses.sentence: That’s a fair point, however the cheap place has a two-hour wait on Fridays.
uses.tip: Casually, “fair point, but” sounds more natural.

uses.sentence: That is a fair point; however, the sample was chosen to reflect our target market.
uses.tip: In formal writing, use a semicolon before “however”.

origin.summary: Uses “fair” in its sense of “just, reasonable”. The word comes from Old English fæger, meaning “beautiful, pleasing”; the “just” sense developed in Middle English.

timeline.text: “Fæger” means beautiful or pleasing.
“Fair” gains the sense of just, honest and reasonable.
“Fair point” becomes a common concession in debate.

cards.pitfall: Starting every reply with “fair point” and never changing your mind makes it sound hollow.

cards.meaning: A polite request to look again at a decision or topic that seemed settled.
cards.nuance: Less confrontational than saying a decision was wrong. Repeatedly revisiting the same decision can look like you won’t accept the outcome.

uses.sentence: Now that legal has flagged the data issue, can we revisit this before we commit?
uses.tip: Give a new reason — it shows you’re not just reopening old arguments.

uses.sentence: Can we revisit the beach idea? I just saw how expensive the flights are.
uses.tip: Pointing to a specific change keeps it fair.

uses.sentence: Given the revised costs, I’d like to ask whether we can revisit last month’s budget decision.
uses.tip: In formal writing, frame it as a request, not a demand.

origin.summary: From Latin revisere, “to look at again”, via French. In English, “revisit” meant returning to a place; the figurative “reconsider a decision” sense became common in modern usage.

timeline.text: “Revisere” means to look back at or visit again.
“Revisit” enters English via French, mainly for places.
Widely used for reconsidering ideas and decisions.

similar: can we look at this again
cards.pitfall: Asking to revisit a decision without new information can feel like relitigating it.

cards.term: Take it with a pinch of salt
cards.meaning: Treat something with doubt, because it may not be completely true or reliable.
cards.nuance: A gentle way to question a claim without calling anyone a liar. Americans more often say “a grain of salt”.

uses.sentence: I’d take their uptime claims with a pinch of salt until we see independent data.
uses.tip: Say what evidence would change your mind.

uses.sentence: Take those five-star reviews with a pinch of salt — half of them were posted the same day.
uses.tip: Giving a reason makes it sound fair, not cynical.

uses.sentence: Early survey results should be taken with a pinch of salt given the small sample size.
uses.tip: In formal writing, “treated with caution” is a plainer option.

origin.summary: Often traced to Pliny the Elder’s recipe for an antidote to poison, taken “with a grain of salt”. The link is plausible but unproven; the doubting sense appears in English much later.

timeline.text: Pliny’s Natural History lists an antidote taken with a grain of salt.
Latin “cum grano salis” used to mean “with some scepticism”.
“With a grain/pinch of salt” becomes common in English.

similar: don’t take it at face value
cards.pitfall: Saying this about a colleague’s own work, to their face, can sound like you think they’re dishonest.

cards.term: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater
cards.meaning: Don’t reject something completely just because part of it is bad; keep what works.
cards.nuance: A friendly, vivid way to argue against an overreaction. It can feel patronising if aimed at someone who has already thought it through.

uses.sentence: The rollout failed, but let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater — the onboarding flow tested really well.
uses.highlight: throw the baby out with the bathwater
uses.tip: Name the “baby” — the part worth keeping.

uses.where: Friend wants to quit the gym
uses.sentence: You hate the classes, fine, but don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater — keep swimming.
uses.highlight: throw the baby out with the bathwater
uses.tip: Works well when someone is about to quit everything.

uses.sentence: Scrapping the whole scheme would throw the baby out with the bathwater.
uses.highlight: throw the baby out with the bathwater
uses.tip: In formal writing, it’s vivid but use it once.

origin.summary: A German proverb first recorded in 1512 in Thomas Murner’s satire Narrenbeschwörung. Thomas Carlyle brought it into English in 1849.

timeline.text: Murner writes “das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten” in Narrenbeschwörung.
Carlyle uses it in an English essay, adapting the German proverb.
A standard English warning against overreacting.

cards.pitfall: A popular claim that it comes from medieval families sharing one bath is a myth — the real source is Murner’s proverb.

cards.term: I’m not sure that’s the best use of our time
cards.meaning: A polite way of saying a task or discussion isn’t worth the time it would take.
cards.nuance: Frames refusal as a question of priorities, not personal dislike. Said about someone’s pet project, it can sound dismissive.

uses.sentence: I’m not sure that’s the best use of our time — nobody has read the last two reports.
uses.highlight: I’m not sure that’s the best use of our time
uses.tip: Suggest what would be a better use of the time.

uses.sentence: I’m not sure that’s the best use of our time when we only have one day in Rome.
uses.highlight: I’m not sure that’s the best use of our time
uses.tip: Linking it to a shared limit (one day) keeps it fair.

uses.sentence: I’m not sure a full audit is the best use of our time before the deadline; could we do a spot check instead?
uses.highlight: the best use of our time
uses.tip: Offer an alternative so it reads as constructive.

origin.summary: Plain modern English with no single origin. It draws on the long-standing idea that time is a resource to spend wisely, famously put by Benjamin Franklin as “time is money” in 1748.

timeline.text: Franklin’s “Advice to a Young Tradesman” says “time is money”.
Management talk frames choices in terms of priorities and opportunity cost.
A common, polite way to decline work in meetings.

similar: I don’t think that’s worth it
cards.pitfall: Without an alternative, it can sound like you just don’t want to do the work.
